newsitem.title: PERU: Standoff continues as rebels 200 hostages in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Standoff continues as rebels 200 hostages in Peru.

text.p: Leftist Peruvian rebels who stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence threatened on Wednesday to kill at least 200 hostages, including high-ranking diplomats, unless the government freed jailed comrades.

"If they do not release our prisoners, we will all die in here," a guerrilla from the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) told a local radio station from within the embassy residence.

The armed stand-off was unresolved after dawn broke at the residence following Tuesday night's spectacular assault during which heavily armed rebels attacked the building from outside while, according to some versions, guerrillas disguised as waiters joined in from the inside.

Juan Carlos Mejia, head of the special police task force handling the siege, confirmed that the rebels had smuggled ammunition into the residency among flowers and Christmas cake. He could not, however, confirm if some rebels had entered dressed as waiters.
A Reuters photographer saw a Christmas cake full of cartridges at the back of the residency.

Speaking freely with local media from within the building, MRTA rebels accused the Peruvian government of "intransigence" and said they had laid explosive booby-traps at the entrances to the building.

"Up to now, there is an intransigent position (from the authorities). The only solution is a political one," MRTA member Walter Loayza said, adding that the rebels wanted transportion for them and the freed prisoners to a guerrilla-controlled area in the jungle.

The hostages included Peru's Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja and ambassadors, diplomats and businessmen from around the world.

The drama began at about 8 p.m. local time Tuesday (0100 GMT) when the guerrillas fired a rocket and sprayed bullets into the residency building before scaling walls and entering during the ensuing chaos, witnesses and officials said.
A series of small explosions and gunfire was heard as the rebels quickly took control of the building in the middle-class, residential San Isidro area of Lima.
The hostages, who were attending a reception to honour the Japanese Emperor's birthday, were forced to lie face-down on the floor for about 40 minutes.

Japan, Germany and Austria confirmed the presence of their ambassadors among the hostages, while the ambassadors of Spain, Cuba, Bolivia, South Korea, Brazil and the European Union were also inside the building according to various reports from witnesses and reporters on the scene.
Wednesday morning, scores of policemen, journalists and onlookers surrounded the luxury residence.

The MRTA guerrillas, who called the operation "Breaking The Silence," claimed they held 250 hostages after the release of about 80 women and old people. One of the released people, Sally Bowen, president of Peru's foreign correspondents' association, said "between 250 and 300" men were still being held inside shortly after midnight local time (0500 GMT).

President Alberto Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, put the number of hostages at 200 in a telephone conversation with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. Fujimori said Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila was negotiating with the guerrillas to seek the release of the hostages, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry.

Bowen said the guerrillas, dressed in black and armed with machine-guns and grenades, were pretty "calm and determined." However, "it was scary, especially during the shooting at the beginning," she said.

The rebels said they had 400 to 500 comrades in jail and insisted their highest priority was the release of Victor Polay, their leader who was imprisoned in 1992. They also called for a review of Peru's judicial system and direct negotiations with the government.
The guerrillas, whose number was estimated at about 20 by officials on the scene, were allowing the hostages to call their families from within the embassy residence.

The released hostages, who included Fujimori's mother apparently freed by mistake, came out of the residence dazed and crying. "They are freeing us to show that they are not doing us any harm," said one woman.

Witnesses said one of the MRTA leaders had a serious bullet wound in his leg, and Akoi appealed via telephone for medical equipment and personnel to be sent in urgently. "The situation is calm, but there are some injuries," he said.
The attack was a major blow to Fujimori's government, which had claimed virtual victory in a 16-year war on communist rebels belonging to the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path.
